title: Giant bulk photovoltaic effect driven by interfacial symmetry breaking in MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 heterostructures
authors: Jianwen Ma, Pengliang Leng, Lei Peng, Congming Hao, Xianghao Meng, Jiaqi Liu, Yang Gan, Min Luo, Zifan Zhang, Jiaming Gu, Qinghang Liu, Lidan Duan, Du Xiang, Wu Shi, Peng Wang, Weibin Chu, Xiang Yuan, Weida Hu, Cheng Zhang
abstract: Van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures offer a versatile platform for engineering unconventional bulk photovoltaic (BPV) effect through interfacial symmetry breaking. However, the coexistence of multiple photophysical mechanisms, driven by structural complexity, spontaneous charge transfer, and strong interlayer coupling, often obscures the microscopic origin of the BPV response and hinders its rational optimization. Here, we demonstrate a pronounced BPV effect localized at the overlap region of a cross-bar MoS2/Ta2NiSe5 vdW heterostructure, where symmetry breaking induced by vertical stacking lifts the inversion center of MoS2. The orthogonal device geometry enables the independent probing of intralayer and interfacial photoresponse pathways, facilitating clear separation of competing mechanisms. Spontaneous interfacial charge transfer between MoS2 and Ta2NiSe5 further establishes a strong interlayer electronic coupling. By modulating the interlayer potential landscape through gate voltage and vertical electric fields, we achieve an optimized zero-bias photocurrent density of 247 A/cm2 and a BPV coefficient of 0.99 V-1. Supported by theoretical modelling, our results illustrate how minimalist device geometry can transform complex heterostructures into experimentally tractable platforms. This strategy paves the way for analyzing and optimizing interface-driven BPV effect, with implications for self-powered optoelectronics, broadband photodetection, and energy-harvesting nanodevices.
summary: This paper reports on achieving a giant bulk photovoltaic effect in a $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{Ta}_2	ext{NiSe}_5$ heterostructure by engineering interfacial symmetry breaking. Using a specialized cross-bar device, the authors successfully separated competing photophysical mechanisms to quantify a high BPV response. This work provides a platform for designing self-powered optoelectronic devices based on interface engineering.
main_problem: The primary challenge is disentangling the microscopic origins and optimizing the bulk photovoltaic (BPV) effect in complex Van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures where multiple photophysical mechanisms overlap.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a giant BPV effect localized at the $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{Ta}_2	ext{NiSe}_5$ interface, achieving a high photocurrent density ($247 	ext{ A/cm}^2$) by exploiting symmetry breaking.
method: The study combines advanced electrical measurements (I-V, photovoltage mapping, gate-tuning) with theoretical modeling (DFT calculations of conductivity tensors).
model_or_system: The physical system is the $	ext{MoS}_2/	ext{Ta}_2	ext{NiSe}_5$ vdW heterostructure, studied using a cross-bar device geometry to isolate interfacial photoresponse.
key_observables: Zero-bias photocurrent density ($247 	ext{ A/cm}^2$), BPV coefficient ($0.99 	ext{ V}^{-1}$), localized photovoltage enhancement, and gate-tunable barrier heights.
important_parameters: Gate voltage ($	ext{V}_{	ext{BG}}$), vertical electric field ($	ext{V}_z$), and laser power density ($P$).
main_assumptions: The cross-bar geometry is crucial as a strategy to spatially separate and independently probe the contributions of interfacial symmetry breaking versus intralayer effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture, the localization of the BPV effect at the overlap region, the dependence of photoresponse on external biases, and comparisons of the BPV coefficient against other materials.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the complex nature of BPV in vdW heterostructures, presenting the cross-bar device setup for controlled measurement, quantifying the giant BPV effect through electrical characterization, and supporting these findings with theoretical calculations of symmetry-dependent charge transport.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state optoelectronics, the concept of engineered symmetry breaking to control electronic response is analogous to controlling coupling terms in open quantum systems or designing tailored quantum interfaces.
